extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalism scholars, editors and professional journalists interested in criteria for selecting and producing foreign news
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and operationalization of factors that determine whether an event becomes foreign news; aimed at explaining selection biases and giving concrete implications for journalists and news organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The more of the defined factors an event satisfies, the higher the probability that it becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat newsworthiness as (approximately) additive across factors — events satisfying many factors are more likely to be selected. Use the set of factors collectively to predict selection rather than any single factor alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The factors will tend to exclude each other since if one factor is present it is less necessary for the other factors to be present for the event to become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate trade-offs among factors: a very strong single factor (e.g., extreme conflict) can substitute for other factors (e.g., unexpectedness). Analysis of selection should consider such complementarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that satisfy none or very few factors will not become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an event meets few of the criteria (frequency, threshold, unexpectedness, continuity, consonance, personification, etc.), it is unlikely to be selected as news; selection mechanisms effectively exclude such events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance / fit with stereotypes (esp. for low-rank nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: (9,5) The lower the rank of the nation, the more consonant (i.e., fitting pre-existing stereotypes or the 'mental pre-image') the news will have to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For low-ranked or culturally distant countries, news items are more likely selected if they confirm stereotyped expectations (e.g., signs of 'immaturity': payment crises, political instability, elite murder). This produces simple, stereotype-confirming reports and under-reports positive or stereotype-challenging material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness by social rank (person-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: (10,6) The lower the rank of the person, the more unexpected the event has to be for that person to make news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elite actors can be reported for routine actions; rank-and-file individuals only make news when something sharply contrasts with their ordinary life (e.g., sudden wealth, extreme wrongdoing). Track deviations from ordinary expectations given the subject's social rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite placement requirement for low-rank nations
rubrics_metrics.description: (9,10) The lower the rank of the nation, the higher the social/political status of the person who must be involved for the event to make news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News from low-ranked countries tends to feature top elites; ordinary people rarely appear unless elevated to elite-level actions. This produces elite-dominated images of underdog nations and weak identification with masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity bias by nation rank
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the nation, the more negative the news from that nation will have to be to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive developments in underdog nations are under-reported; negative events (coups, disasters) dominate coverage, reinforcing images of incapacity or danger (examples: Latin American coups, disaster reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity bias by person rank
rubrics_metrics.description: (10,12) The lower the rank of a person, the more negative his actions must be to make news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common people generally enter news pages through negative acts (crime); positive actions by ordinary people seldom satisfy criteria (frequency, threshold, unexpectedness, continuity) and thus rarely make news unless exceptional (sport, arts) or presented as feature stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization vs. impersonal causation
rubrics_metrics.description: (11,12) The less personal the news (i.e., attributed to non-personal causes), the more negative it will have to be to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive outcomes are more likely attributed to people; events attributed to impersonal causes (nature, structural factors) must be negative (disasters, crises) to reach news. This reflects cultural notions of agency and the news value of human agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification / meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: News is more meaningful (and thus more likely to be selected) if it allows the audience to identify with the event or persons involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favors events that provide identification with the reader or their nation/group; meaningfulness is tied to identification and familiarity, so distance reduces perceived meaningfulness unless other factors compensate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are predictable and/or frequent can be worth reporting to counterbalance an overly event-driven, dramatic image of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should sometimes emphasize predictable and frequent occurrences to provide balance; selection processes often undervalue the routine despite its social importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold / Just Noticeable Difference (jnd)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more dramatic the existing context (higher background 'signal'), the larger the increment required for an event to be noticed as news (jnd/threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very dramatic environment raises the threshold for what new events will register as news; this can produce escalating exaggeration because more must be added to capture attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity / follow-up requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of continuity increases newsworthiness; follow-ups on events are necessary even if long gaps interrupt the chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News selection should value continuity and include follow-ups to avoid presenting events as isolated flashes; failure to follow up can bias the public image of an event or country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition factor (avoid creating news artefacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of what is reported (mix of event types, geographic focus, actors) can create artificial impressions ('news artefacts').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms should be aware of how sampling and composition choices (which papers/regions/agents covered) shape perceived patterns; deliberate balancing can reduce artefacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification / role of elite concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: News favors personification and concentration on elites; reporting tends to centre on elite actors and elite nations who are 'topdogs' and their 'underlings'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect over-representation of elite individuals and topdog nations; under-representation of ordinary people and peripheral countries unless they involve elites or dramatic exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural distance and relatedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events from culturally distant zones are less likely to be covered unless tied to the audience's own country or framed as relevant to the centre; reporting often ties remote events to one’s own national interests (relatedness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To broaden coverage, editors should deliberately include reports from culturally distant areas even where immediate relevance is low; exchanges of local columns and background reporting can help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias toward conflict over conciliation (developed countries)
rubrics_metrics.description: In coverage of developed countries, conflict tends to be emphasized and conciliation downplayed; foreign issues show higher ranking on policies of force compared to domestic issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to systematic emphasis on conflict in foreign reporting; consider balancing with coverage of conciliation and mutual adjustment when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined stereotype effect for distant & low-rank countries
rubrics_metrics.description: When cultural distance and low international rank coincide, news from such countries tends to be: about people (preferably elites), negative and unexpected, consonant with mental pre-images, simple, and offering identification where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combination reinforces images of periphery nations as dangerous or elite-dominated; reporters should be cautious of this compound bias and actively seek dissonant, complex, and positive stories to counter it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 1: Emphasize build-up and background material
rubrics_metrics.description: More emphasis on build-up and background material in total media output; journalists should be trained to capture and report long-term development and concentrate less on isolated 'events'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement training and editorial practices that privilege context, trends, and development over event-driven reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 2: Report occasional trivial items
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional reports on the trivial even if they do not make 'news' to counterbalance the image of the world as composed of strings of dramatic events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include human-interest and everyday-life pieces to avoid an exclusively drama- and crisis-focused public image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 3: Cover complex and ambiguous events
rubrics_metrics.description: More emphasis on complex and ambiguous events, not necessarily with any effort to interpret them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report complexity and ambiguity without forcing simplified interpretations; allow readers access to nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 4: Increase coverage of culturally distant zones
rubrics_metrics.description: More reports from culturally distant zones even if the content has no immediate relevance; experiment with newspaper exchanges of local columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exchanges, correspondents, and commissioning to diversify geographical and cultural coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 5: Emphasize dissonant information
rubrics_metrics.description: More emphasis on the dissonant — that which does not fit stereotypes; train journalists to increase their insight into their own stereotypes to reduce consonance bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop training modules and editorial checks aimed at identifying and countering stereotypical framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 6: Emphasize predictable and frequent events
rubrics_metrics.description: More emphasis given to predictable and frequent occurrences to counterbalance the over-focus on dramatic irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule routine reporting on frequent phenomena (economic trends, governance routines) to give a fuller picture of societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 7: Improve awareness of continuity and provide follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: More awareness of continuity — and more emphasis on follow-ups even if the chain of events has been interrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should mandate follow-ups on previously covered events to show aftermaths and counteract one-off dramatic framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 8: Be aware of composition effects
rubrics_metrics.description: More awareness of the composition factor in order not to create news artefacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor the overall mix of stories (by geography, theme, actor) to avoid skewed impressions produced by selective sampling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 9: More coverage of non-elite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase coverage of nations that are not topdog/elite to reduce center-periphery distortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate reporting resources and commissioning to produce more balanced geographic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 10: More coverage of non-elite people
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase reporting on ordinary people, not only elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use beat reporting, human-interest stories, and feature journalism to surface everyday actors and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 11: Reference non-personal causes more
rubrics_metrics.description: More reference to non-personal causes of events; special training is probably needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train journalists to identify and report structural, environmental, and systemic causes (not only human agency) and to present them in accessible ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy recommendation 12: Report positive events more
rubrics_metrics.description: More reference to positive events to counterbalance overwhelmingly negative portrayals of peripheral countries and people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek and publish constructive, developmental, and positive stories that challenge prevailing negativity bias.
